splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA must be finalized. The timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay, affecting billions of dollars in potential obligations across thousands of multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, so long as the assumptions are applied to data as of that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year) to provide employers with predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to create such a doctrine.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the stricter gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars re-raising previously presented claims — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any previously presented claim, in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners under § 2255, who need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome affects whether election-rule challenges can be litigated before elections take place or must wait until after, with significant implications for mail-in voting and ballot counting deadlines nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election because of the competitive injury caused by laws that may affect voting procedures and outcomes.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election administration procedures pre-election absent a concrete, particularized injury beyond generalized competitive concerns.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations in the criminal context. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has gained importance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in the criminal context, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing deference to anti-defendant readings of ambiguous Guidelines enhancements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the safety-valve provision. This determines whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether possessing any one is disqualifying, significantly affecting mandatory minimum sentencing across the country.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is disqualifying from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text itself does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid, authoritative interpretation of the guideline under Stinson/Kisor deference. The split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is the Sentencing Commission's authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline, and conspiracy qualifies as a controlled substance offense for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds the guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' beyond what the text allows.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are sharply divided on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered as a basis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes can never serve as a basis, while others allow courts to consider them as one factor among many. The split has deepened as the Sentencing Commission's new policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) explicitly permits it.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as one factor among others when evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant a sentence reduction.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to a Hyde Amendment order for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil deadline) or part of the criminal case (triggering the shorter 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and thus the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case and the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not also controlled under federal law.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires a match with federally controlled substances or encompasses any substance controlled under state law. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-match requirement
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is controlled under federal law.

positions.label: Federal-match requirement applies
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under federal law.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. De La Rosa

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust and the need to protect the public.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of a sentence imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to punish for the violation itself, while other circuits limit the sentence to addressing the breach of trust in the supervisory relationship. This affects hundreds of revocations each year.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing the Sixth Circuit at the extreme of the circuit split.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is not permissible
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should address the breach of trust inherent in the violation and the need to protect the public, not punish the underlying conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held such appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that hold it belongs to the debtor under § 348(f)(1)(A).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), coupled with the broad scope of § 541(a), means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under the Bankruptcy Code's structure, post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors to protect their incentive to attempt reorganization under Chapter 13.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or execution of their confinement exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether they may also use civil rights statutes such as Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions or execution of confinement, or whether civil rights actions are also available. The split has evolved over decades and affects prisoners challenging BOP decisions on matters like First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges affecting duration
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge effectively seeks earlier release, habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy, precluding civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring challenges to conditions of confinement through civil rights actions even when habeas may also be available, particularly when the challenge does not directly seek release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of racial discrimination in the operation of hotels and hospitality establishments under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 and related civil rights statutes?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality settings was found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review, suggesting a circuit split on the standards for proving discrimination liability and available remedies in service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that plaintiffs may establish discrimination claims under § 1981 in hospitality settings with less direct evidence of discriminatory intent, allowing broader theories of liability.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that discrimination claims in hospitality settings require more direct evidence of discriminatory intent and applies more restrictive standards for establishing liability.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal medical records filed in a pending litigation is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether denials of motions to seal medical information qualify as immediately appealable collateral orders under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, creating tension with circuits that take a narrower view of the collateral order doctrine in sealing cases.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal medical records are effectively unreviewable on final appeal and involve a value of sufficiently high order to warrant immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because adequate alternative remedies exist, such as seeking mandamus or raising the issue on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier,' extends to common-law negligence claims against freight brokers. This affects the liability framework for the freight brokerage industry nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted because they are general common-law duties of care rather than laws specifically 'related to' broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Post-Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal ban on firearm possession by unlawful drug users passes constitutional muster under the Second Amendment's historical-tradition test. Some circuits have upheld § 922(g)(3) as consistent with historical traditions of disarming dangerous persons, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of disarming those who pose a danger to themselves or others, and survives Second Amendment scrutiny even as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government cannot identify a sufficient historical tradition of disarming persons solely for drug use.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether legal errors or constitutional claims that could have been raised in a § 2255 habeas petition may also serve as the basis for compassionate release. Some circuits permit courts to consider such claims as one factor, while others hold that compassionate release cannot be used as a substitute for habeas review.

positions.label: May consider conviction-related errors
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not be used as a vehicle to challenge the validity of a conviction or sentence, as those claims must be raised through § 2255 habeas proceedings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
